title: An Inspector Calls GCSE Revision: Themes, Characters, Context & Essay Planning
description: Revise An Inspector Calls for GCSE English Literature with themes, characters, dramatic methods, social context, whole-play links and practical essay-planning.

children: An Inspector Calls is stronger when revised as a deliberately constructed drama rather than a list of characters. Priestley controls entrances, exits, revelations, lighting, timing and the final twist to test the characters' beliefs about responsibility.
Core themes
Social responsibility and collective obligation.
Class, wealth and economic power.
Gender and the treatment of women.
Generational conflict and the possibility of change.
Capitalism, individualism and socialist alternatives.
Reputation, hypocrisy and public versus private morality.
Revise relationships, not isolated profiles

Trace contrasts. Mr Birling and the Inspector embody competing ideas about society; Sheila and Eric change more visibly than their parents; Gerald shows sympathy but is also drawn back towards the older generation's relief once the Inspector's identity is questioned.
Dramatic methods to analyse
Opening stage directions establish comfort, status and self-satisfaction before disruption.
Entrances and exits allow information to be revealed in a controlled sequence.
The Inspector's questioning links separate actions into one chain of consequences.
Dramatic irony undermines confident claims that the audience knows are wrong.
The final telephone call prevents the family from dismissing the moral lesson simply because they think they solved the mystery.
Context that illuminates the play

The play is set in 1912 but first performed in the mid-1940s. That gap lets Priestley present pre-war confidence, rigid hierarchy and individualism to an audience that had lived through two world wars and greater collective sacrifice. Context matters when it helps explain the force of a dramatic choice.
Build essays around change and contrast
Who accepts responsibility and who resists it?
Who changes, and how securely?
How does Priestley make the audience judge wealth and status?
How are younger and older characters used differently?
How does the Inspector connect private actions to a wider social argument?
Practical essay plan

Start with a thesis that answers the exact wording. Plan three conceptual paragraphs rather than three quotations. Each paragraph should make one claim, use precise textual reference, analyse a dramatic or language choice, and connect the detail to Priestley's larger argument.
Common mistakes
Retelling Eva Smith's chronology instead of analysing how Priestley reveals it.
Treating context as a separate paragraph about capitalism and socialism.
Ignoring stage directions because they are not dialogue.
Saying a character merely represents an idea without analysing how the drama makes that representation persuasive.
Assuming the ending cancels the Inspector's message; structurally, it renews the consequences.
